A release has two steps, in this order: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets are never deleted as part of the release.

**Why upload comes first:** The manifest is the only thing that tells a browser which files to load. Once it changes, any browser that fetches it will immediately request the new names. If those files aren't uploaded yet, those requests 404 and the page breaks. Uploading first guarantees that every name the new manifest mentions already exists. Because the new files have new names, uploading them doesn't touch anything the live site uses. The only step users can see is the manifest switch, which happens in one step.

**Why old assets stay:** Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the old one. A tab opened before the release still holds the old manifest and will keep requesting old asset names as it lazy-loads routes, chunks, images, or fonts. If those files were gone, a user in the middle of a session would get broken pages until they reloaded. Keeping the old files lets both versions work at the same time. Users already on the site keep the release they started with, and new visitors get the new one.

The versioned names are what make this safe. Each release's files sit at their own names, so the two releases never overwrite each other, and caches can hold any asset indefinitely because a given name always means the same content.

Each release ships in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.4f2c.js`, and then we update the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes before the switch so the manifest never references a file that doesn't exist yet. Once the manifest changes, any browser can fetch it and immediately request the new asset names. If those files aren't already in place, that browser gets 404s and a broken page. Because the files are already there when the switch happens, the release takes effect atomically: a visitor gets either the complete old version or the complete new one.

We keep the old assets because the switch doesn't reach browsers that already have the previous manifest. A page opened before the release will still request old asset names, for example when lazy-loading a chunk or navigating. If we deleted those files, those sessions would break partway through. Keeping the old assets lets every browser finish with the version it started on.

Versioned names are what make both steps safe. New files never overwrite old ones, so both versions can sit side by side.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never references a file that doesn't exist yet. If we switched first, any browser that fetched the new manifest before the uploads finished would request missing assets and get a broken page. Once every versioned file is already in place, the switch is safe at any moment.

We keep the old assets because some browsers already loaded the previous manifest and will keep requesting the files it lists, sometimes long after the switch. Because every version has its own filenames, the old files can stay alongside the new ones without conflict. Those browsers keep working until they pick up the new manifest.

Our releases are ordered so that every browser always sees a consistent set of files, whichever version it loaded.

**How it works**

1. Upload every new asset under a versioned name. Because each version gets its own names, the upload never overwrites anything the live site uses.
2. Switch the manifest to point at the new names. This one change is the release.
3. Leave the old assets in place.

**Why the upload comes first**

A browser that fetches the new manifest immediately requests the files it names. If we switched the manifest first, those requests could reach files that hadn't finished uploading and fail, breaking the page for anyone who loaded during that window. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists the moment the manifest goes live. Until then, the new files sit unused alongside the live ones.

**Why we keep the old assets**

The switch doesn't reach browsers that already fetched the previous manifest. They keep requesting the old names. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would get failed requests even though nothing was wrong on their end. Keeping the old assets lets them carry on with the version they started on, while new visitors get the new one.
